summary: The board's own logic is essentially the RCA CDP1869/1870 VIS video/sound pair plus glue, and the core rebuilds it the way MAME's cdp1869 device and the cidelsa_v.cpp callbacks describe it rather than as the chip's internal counters. The CPU-side char/PCB RAM addressing is MAME's cidelsa_charram_r/w expression nearly verbatim, PCB-to-IN0 goes through a latched side-effect copy of m_cdp1869_pcb, and the video path uses MAME's derived quantities (rows from integer division, pmemsize wrap, ccb0/ccb1/pcb pen selection, 8+64 pen palette with luma weights). Rendering does scan pixel by pixel off H/V counters, but that's normal FPGA practice and doesn't argue for hardware structure; the only real hardware-flavoured detail is the Draco COP402-to-AY pin wiring.

findings.signal: char RAM address = MAME callback expression
findings.note: `column = pma_c[10] ? 8'hff : pmd_cpu; char_idx = ((column << 3) | (cma & 3'd7)) & 11'h7ff` is MAME's `BIT(pma,10) ? 0xff : pmd; ((column << 3) | (cma & 0x07)) & CIDELSA_CHARRAM_MASK` with the same variable names. The Draco variant drops the PMA10 test exactly as draco_charram_r does.

findings.signal: PCB read modelled as callback side-effect latch
findings.note: A register pcb_in0 is loaded whenever the CPU reads char RAM and then shows up as IN0 bit 7. That copies MAME's m_cdp1869_pcb, which charram_r sets as a side effect and the IN0 PORT_CUSTOM reads back. It does not model the PCB bit sitting on a bus or the CDP1852 input latch (ic23).

findings.signal: CMEM/PMA/CMA address logic in MAME device terms
findings.mame_ref: MAME cdp1869 device (char_map/page_map handlers; file not provided, recalled)
findings.note: Names and logic (`get_pma`, `pma = cmem ? get_pma : offset`, `cma` masked to 3 bits when dblpage) follow the emulator's read/write handler helpers. A gate-level decode of the VIS address pins would look different.

findings.mame_ref: MAME cdp1869 device screen_update (rows = visible lines / height)
findings.note: The row-count table (8->27, 9->24, 16->13, 18->12, 32->6) is the value of (260-44+1)/height. in_grid clips the partial last row, which reproduces a software loop bound rather than a chip row counter running until the display window ends.

findings.mame_ref: MAME cdp1869 device get_pmemsize / screen_update addr wrap
findings.note: The page address is computed as hma + row*cols + col, and when it reaches pmemsize = cols*rows*(dblpage?2:1)*(line16?2:1) it wraps by subtracting pmemsize, using the emulator's variable name and formula. A real chip would use an incrementing address counter.
ccb0=bit6, ccb1=bit7, and the COL case table assigning ccb0/ccb1/pcb to r/b/g, followed by `cfc ? color + ((bkg+1)<<3) : color`, matches MAME's get_pen, including its names and pen-offset arithmetic.

findings.signal: palette indices and luma weights from MAME palette init
findings.mame_ref: MAME cdp1869 device palette init / get_rgb
findings.note: The colour is encoded into a 7-bit pen index (8 full-luma pens plus 64 colour x luma pens) and then decoded again by `(pen-8)>>3` and `(pen-8)&7`. The luma table 150/28/76 is 59%/11%/30% of 255, so this round-trips through MAME's palette layout instead of driving the 1870's RGB/luminance outputs directly.

findings.signal: video timing constants are MAME device constants
findings.note: The windows (360/336/324/30/54/300, 312/308/304/10/44/260, predisplay 43-260) come from pixel-count comparators on flat counters with MAME-style START/END names. There are no character-clock divider or counter-chain taps.

OUT3 takes data while OUT4-7 take the address bus, and Cidelsa routes inverted PRD to INT+EF1 while Draco routes PRD to EF1 only. A correct core has to share these with the emulator; the decomposition into one register file module mirrors cdp1869_w -> out3_w..out7_w, though the datasheet would give the same.

Page, char and PCB RAMs are fetched per character cell from H/V counters, with a 2-stage pipeline delaying pixel select and sync. This is a raster-time pipeline rather than a frame batch, but it is standard FPGA practice and isn't organised around the chip's internals.

The tone divisor `512 >> tonefreq` * (tonediv+1) and the noise divisor `4096 >> wnfreq` match both the datasheet and MAME's frequency formulas. The noise uses a generic 17-bit LFSR that comes from neither source.

findings.signal: COP402 G pins drive AY BDIR/BC1 directly
findings.note: G0/G1 are wired straight to the AY's bdir/bc1 pins and the AY data bus is fed from the COP Q port. MAME instead uses a switch over G values plus an m_psg_latch software latch on the L port, so this follows the physical bus more than the driver. Draco only, though.
